n: Church of the Holy Archangels Michael and Gabriel
w: Built in the 13th or 14th century, this partially preserved Eastern Orthodox church forms part of the Ancient Nesebar UNESCO World Heritage Site. A single-nave design with three apses, it once carried a dome and bell tower, its exterior richly decorated in Nesebar's characteristic style.
s: A part-ruined Byzantine church on Nesebar's rock
_facts: Medieval Eastern Orthodox church built 13th-14th century
Part of the Ancient Nesebar UNESCO World Heritage Site
Single-nave church with three apses; dome and bell tower now lost

w: Likely raised in the 13th or 14th century, the Church of Saint Paraskevi is one of the medieval churches of the Ancient Nesebar UNESCO site. It has a single nave and a pentagonal apse, richly decorated outside, though its dome and belfry are lost, and which of three saints named Paraskevi it honours remains unknown.
s: Nesebar church, dedicated to an uncertain Paraskevi
_facts: Medieval Eastern Orthodox church, likely 13th-14th century
Single nave with a pentagonal apse
Dedication among three saints named Paraskevi is unresolved

w: Built in the 13th century, the Church of St Theodore keeps its original north and west facades, though later builders replaced the other walls and roof. This single-nave church, just 8.7 by 4.15 metres, wears Nesebar's signature decor: blind arches filled with zigzag stone-and-brick patterns.
s: Zigzag brick and stone on a tiny 13th-century church
_facts: Built in the 13th century; north and west facades original
Single nave with narthex and apse, 8.70m by 4.15m
Facade decorated with blind arches and zigzag brick-and-stone patterns

w: Raised in 1609 in Nesebar's old town, the Church of the Holy Saviour is a small single-nave building, 11.7 by 5.7 metres, notable for early wall paintings of Christ and the Virgin. Deconsecrated, it now doubles as a museum; a Byzantine princess's tombstone once kept here has since moved to the archaeological museum.
s: Nesebar church turned museum, minus its royal tomb
_facts: Built in 1609, 11.70m by 5.70m, single nave and apse
Early 17th-century wall paintings of the life of Christ and the Virgin
Now deconsecrated and used as a museum
Formerly held the tombstone of Byzantine princess Mataissa Cantacuzina
